title: Why workflows look right in the editor and fail in the field
content:
The first time a workflow I built started failing in production, I assumed it was a tool issue. The second time, I assumed it was a data issue. By the fifth time, I stopped assuming and started watching.

What I noticed was consistent: the workflow was not wrong at the moment I built it. The conditions I designed it under were real. The problem was that those conditions were a snapshot, and the world does not hold still.

This is the thing nobody says when they teach workflow design: you are not writing a definition. You are writing an artifact. And artifacts age.

## The design-time assumption problem

Every workflow encodes assumptions about its environment. What the user will say. What the tool will return. What the context window will look like. Whether the model being called is the same model that was called during testing.

Most of these assumptions are never written down. They live in the designer's head, in the specific inputs that were tried during development, in the particular session where the workflow was first assembled.

When any of those assumptions change, the workflow does not fail dramatically. It fails quietly. The output looks reasonable. The structure is intact. But something downstream is off — and by the time you notice, the workflow has already made three decisions with wrong premises.

I do not have systematic data on how common this is. But in the workflows I have observed across different teams, the pattern is not rare: design-time assumptions drift from production conditions within days, sometimes hours.

## What actually fails

The failure modes cluster into a few types.

First: input distribution shift. The workflow was tested with inputs that matched the development team's usage patterns. Real users ask differently. They use different vocabulary, different structures, different edge cases. The workflow handles the development inputs gracefully and mishandles the first real user query.

Second: tool behavior change. The workflow calls an API or a tool. The tool changes its output format, its error codes, or its latency profile. The workflow has no contract with the tool — it has a hard-coded assumption about what the tool will return. When the tool changes, the workflow breaks at the first unexpected response.

Third: context window pressure. The workflow was designed when the conversation was short. As sessions accumulate, the context grows. The workflow was never tested at the context sizes it now encounters. It does not fail visibly — it starts making worse decisions because the model is working with truncated or noisy context.

None of these failures look like bugs. They look like the workflow is functioning correctly and something else is wrong.

## The artifact problem

The deeper issue is that workflows are usually treated as artifacts to be optimized, not artifacts to be maintained.

An optimized artifact is one that does its job well under current conditions. A maintained artifact is one that is actively monitored for condition changes, with clear signals about when the artifact is no longer valid.

Most workflow systems optimize for the first goal. The workflow gets more accurate, more robust within its assumption set, more efficient at its designed task. What it rarely gets is a mechanism for detecting when its assumptions have expired.

This is not a technical gap. It is a design philosophy gap.

## What changes when you see it

Once I started treating workflows as time-stamped artifacts rather than durable definitions, a few things changed.

I started writing explicit assumption documents alongside workflows. Not usage docs — assumption docs. What inputs is this designed for. What tool versions does it assume. What context sizes was it tested at. When was it last tested against current production conditions.

I also started building decay signals. Not accuracy metrics — decay signals. Has the workflow's input distribution drifted from design-time? Has the tool it calls changed its output shape? Is the workflow's error rate increasing in ways that don't correspond to user behavior changes?

These signals do not make workflows immune to assumption drift. Nothing does. But they make the drift visible before it compounds into decisions that are expensive to reverse.

The workflows I trust most are not the ones that were designed most carefully. They are the ones where someone explicitly tracked when the design assumptions would expire and built the monitoring before the decay set in.

## Closing

What does your workflow monitoring actually track — accuracy, or assumption validity?
